SE for Proportions:
\[SE=\sqrt{\frac{\pi(1-\pi)}{n}}\]

SE for Means:
\[SE=\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]

Standardized Statistic (SS)



SS for Proportions:
\[z=\frac{\hat{p}-\pi}{SE}\]
\[=\frac{\hat{p}-\pi}{\sqrt{\frac{\pi(1-\pi)}{n}}}\]

SS for Means:
\[t=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu}{SE}\]
\[=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu}{\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}}\]

title: Chapter P
text:
The Six-Step Method Overview

Ask a research question
Design a study and collect data
Explore the data
Draw inferences beyond the data
Formulate conclusions
Look back and ahead

title: Chapter P
text:
1. Ask a research question

What do you want to know or investigate?
It does not have to be super specific

Helper vs. Hinderer example:

Do babies show a preference for the helper toy or the hinderer toy after being shown a puppet show?

We’re REALLY investigating nature vs. nurture

title: Chapter P
section: 2. Design a study and collect data
text:
2. Design a study and collect data

How will you test for your question?
What kind of data should be collected?

Helper vs. Hinderer example:

Recruit babies
Show each baby the puppet show
Record which toy the baby chooses

title: Chapter P
text:
3. Explore the data

Visually: Create boxplots, histograms, other graphs/charts
Numerically: Compute a number

Helper vs. Hinderer example:

14 picked the helper, 2 picked the hinderer

Proportionally: 14/16 = 0.875

title: Chapter P
text:
4. Draw inferences beyond the data

What might our results imply?
Did our data result from chance alone?
Is there an underlying cause?

Helper vs. Hinderer example:

Is 14/16 large enough to conclude babies prefer the helper toy?
Did 14 choose the helper by chance?

Perhaps the puppet show had an influence.

title: Chapter P
text:
5. Formulate conclusions

Strong evidence = form a conclusion
Weak evidence = data was inconclusive
Can often generalize to a population

Helper vs. Hinderer example

Conclusion: Babies preferred the helper toy over the hinderer toy, when shown the puppet show.
Can we say this about all babies?

title: Chapter P
text:
6. Look back and ahead

What was good about the experiment?
What could be improved?
Future research?

Helper vs. Hinderer example:

Recruit more babies

title: Chapter P
text:
Four Pillars of Statistical Evidence

Significance: How strong is the evidence of an effect?
Estimation: What is the size of the effect?
Generalization: How broadly do conclusions apply?
Causation: Can we say what caused the observed difference?


Typically, the pillars apply during step 4 or 5 of the six-step process.

title: Section 3.2
text:
Standard Deviation vs. Standard Error

Standard deviation (SD) is how much a data point is likely to vary from the mean of the data
We can also obtain SD for our null distribution

This is standard error!

Standard error (SE) is how much a sample proportion (or mean) is likely to vary from the true population proportion (or mean)

Formulas for standard error differ for numerical vs. categorical data

title: Section 3.2
text:
Calculating a 2SD Confidence Interval


\hat{p}=\frac{408}{800}=0.51
n=800
SE=\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}*(1-\hat{p})}{n}}=\sqrt{\frac{0.51*(1-0.51)}{800}}=0.0177
CI=\hat{p}±2*SE=0.51±2*0.0177
Lower Bound: 0.51-2*0.0177=0.47
Upper Bound: 0.51+2*0.0177=0.55



Note that this is really close to what we got earlier!

title: Section 3.2
text:

If the observed statistic seems unlikely:

There’s probably some underlying cause

Standardized Statistic for Two Groups
Note that the standard error for the previous statistic uses the combined proportion of success (\hat{p})
\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})(\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2})}
Under the null, we assume \hat{p}_1=\hat{p}_2, so we estimate with \hat{p}, the pooled proportion of success

This is also referred to as pooled standard error

title: Section 5.3
text:
Confidence Interval for Two Groups
General confidence interval formula:
CI=Observed\: Statistic\: ± Multiplier*SE
When comparing two groups:
CI=(\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2)±2*\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1}+\frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}

Interpretation remains essentially the same

title: Section 5.3

Notice that our SE formula differs slightly
\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1}+\frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}
Now, we are assuming that \hat{p}_1≠\hat{p}_2, so we no longer use the pooled standard error.
